text:
Every chart is an argument about the numbers under it. Here are six weeks of tickets, as a pie. Nothing on it is false, and it tells you nothing. Draw the same six numbers as a line, and the story is there before you read a label. That's what these interviews test: choosing the chart, not misleading anyone, and telling the story. There are twenty-two questions. We'll draw seventeen of them twice, the wrong way and the right way, and finish with five short ones. First, how to pick.

Question one. How do you choose the right chart for a question? Start from the question, not the chart. Change over time is a line. Comparing categories is a bar. A part of a whole is a stacked bar. A distribution is a histogram or a box plot. And a relationship is a scatter. Under all of it is how accurately people read each encoding. Position comes first, then length, angle and area, and color last, at about three times the error of position. Two choices come up in almost every interview.

Question two. Line chart or bar chart? It's a question about the x axis. A line says the value passed through everything in between, which is true of weeks. Bars work over weeks too. But put six issue types on the axis, and a line draws a trend through categories that have no order. That's the one wrong chart of the four. Question three. When is a pie chart appropriate? For a few slices of one whole, two to four. Here are five shares. On the pie, S U V and truck look the same. Sorted as bars, the one and a half point gap between them is plain. And never use pies to compare groups, or a share over time. Next, two charts that look alike and aren't.
